name: Zlatko Saračević
milestone_by_age_26: Won the 1986 World Championship gold medal with Yugoslavia at age 25, having already won the Yugoslav Championship (1981) and Yugoslav Cup (1979) with RK Borac Banja Luka and the IHF Junior World Championship gold (1981).
early_history_summary: Saračević was a product of the RK Borac Banja Luka youth academy in Banja Luka, Bosnia-Herzegovina. He began his senior club career at age 16 in 1977, won the Yugoslav Cup at 18 and the Yugoslav Championship at 20, and was part of the Yugoslav junior team that won the 1981 World Junior Championship. He debuted for the senior Yugoslavia national team in 1981 and won the 1986 World Championship at age 25.
family_context_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. Born in Banja Luka, present-day Bosnia and Herzegovina.
primary_early_advantage_tags: youth academy, national team pipeline, Yugoslav handball system, Borac Banja Luka
evidence_summary: Saračević emerged from the RK Borac Banja Luka youth academy, a top Yugoslav handball club, and reached the senior team at 16. By 20 he was a Yugoslav champion and junior world champion, embedded in the dominant Yugoslav handball system that produced multiple world and Olympic titles. No family background or financial details are documented in reviewed sources. His early advantage was primarily institutional: the Borac Banja Luka academy and the Yugoslav national team pipeline provided elite coaching, competition, and teammates from a young age.
starting_point: Born in Banja Luka, Bosnia-Herzegovina; family background not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Died in 2021 at age 59; final role was head coach of RK Podravka in Croatia.

trajectory.event: Won the Yugoslav Cup with RK Borac Banja Luka.
Won the Yugoslav Championship with Borac Banja Luka and the IHF Junior World Championship gold with Yugoslavia U-21.
Won the World Championship gold medal with the Yugoslavia national team.
Won Olympic bronze with Yugoslavia at the Seoul Olympics.
Won Olympic gold with Croatia at the Atlanta Olympics.
Died of cardiac arrest after coaching a domestic league match for RK Podravka.

name: Max Richter
milestone_by_age_26: Co-founded the contemporary classical ensemble Piano Circus in 1989 at age 23, which was signed to Decca/Argo and commissioned and performed works by Arvo Pärt, Brian Eno, Philip Glass, Steve Reich, and Julia Wolfe, producing five albums over a decade.
early_history_summary: Richter grew up in Bedford, England after his family moved from Germany when he was young. He had piano lessons as a child, discovered electronic and minimalist music as a teenager, and studied composition at the University of Edinburgh and the Royal Academy of Music before studying with Luciano Berio in Florence. After finishing his studies in 1989, he co-founded Piano Circus, a six-pianist ensemble that became his primary creative vehicle through his twenties.
family_context_summary: Father was a mechanical engineer and mother was a housewife; family was not artistic. Parents played Bach and Beatles records in the home. Family moved from Germany to Bedford, England when Richter was around three years old.
parent_family_domain_summary: No parental domain expertise in music; father was a mechanical engineer, mother a housewife. The household exposed Richter to classical records but no professional music training was inherited.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Royal Academy of Music, Luciano Berio, Piano Circus, Decca/Argo, Edinburgh University
evidence_summary: Richter benefited from elite institutional training at the University of Edinburgh, the Royal Academy of Music, and with Luciano Berio in Florence, which gave him both technical depth and network access. His parents were not artistic (father was an engineer, mother a housewife), but the family home exposed him to classical music. He was bullied as a German child in England, which may have driven him inward toward music. Co-founding Piano Circus at 23 provided a professional platform signed to Decca/Argo, enabling him to commission and perform works by major minimalist composers through his twenties.
starting_point: Born to a middle-class family in Hamelin, Germany; father was a mechanical engineer, mother a housewife; family moved to Bedford, England when he was around three.
current_position: Active composer and pianist; one of the most prominent contemporary classical composers with over 1 billion streams and 1 million album sales; nominated for an Academy Award in 2026 for Hamnet.

trajectory.event: Co-founded the contemporary classical ensemble Piano Circus, signed to Decca/Argo, commissioning works by major minimalist composers.
Released solo debut album Memoryhouse with the BBC Philharmonic, hailed as a neoclassical masterpiece.
Released The Blue Notebooks, later named one of the best classical works of the century by The Guardian.
Released Recomposed by Max Richter: Vivaldi – The Four Seasons, a major crossover hit.
Released Sleep, an eight-hour overnight work described as the most streamed classical record of all time.
Nominated for an Academy Award for the soundtrack of Hamnet.

name: Ron Arad
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Arad was still a student at the Architectural Association School of Architecture in London (1974-1979) and had not yet produced any notable work. His breakthrough came at age 30 with the 1981 Rover chair.
early_history_summary: Arad was born in Tel Aviv to a progressive Jewish family where both parents were artists. He studied at the Bezalel Academy of Arts and Design in Jerusalem (1971-1973) and then at the Architectural Association School of Architecture in London (1974-1979). After graduating, he briefly worked as an interior architect under Peter Cook before co-founding the design studio One Off in 1981.
family_context_summary: Born in Tel Aviv to a progressive Jewish family; both parents were artists. His mother was a painter who encouraged him toward architecture.
parent_family_domain_summary: Both parents were artists, providing early exposure to creative professions and design thinking.
evidence_summary: Arad was still a student during his early twenties, studying at the Architectural Association in London from 1974 to 1979. His career breakthrough came at age 30 with the Rover chair in 1981, which made him famous overnight. Both parents were artists, giving him early creative exposure, but no material milestone occurred by age 26.

name: Pedro Rodríguez
milestone_by_age_26: Won the 1961 Paris 1000km endurance race with his brother Ricardo at age 21, and made his Formula One world championship debut in 1963 at age 23, having competed internationally in sports cars since 1957.
early_history_summary: Rodríguez was born into a wealthy Mexican family in Mexico City. He began racing competitively at age 8 on bicycles, won national motorcycle championships at ages 12 and 14, and made his international car racing debut at 17 driving a Ferrari at Nassau. He competed at Le Mans for the first time at 18 and won the 1961 Paris 1000km with his brother Ricardo, establishing himself as an international racing driver well before 26.
family_context_summary: Born to a wealthy and powerful Mexican family; father Pedro Natalio Rodríguez was a successful railroad broker and former driver for presidential candidate Lázaro Cárdenas. The family had a comfortable life in Mexico City.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was not a racer but was a racing enthusiast who encouraged competition, signed the boys up for boxing and bicycle racing, and funded their motorcycle and car racing careers.
primary_early_advantage_tags: wealthy family, Ferrari access, brother Ricardo, early racing, NART connection
evidence_summary: Rodríguez came from a wealthy Mexican family that fully supported his racing career from childhood. His father funded motorcycles, cars, and international competition, and had connections that provided access to Ferrari vehicles through NART. Pedro and his brother Ricardo formed a formidable racing partnership, with Ricardo considered a prodigy. Pedro was a national motorcycle champion at 12, raced internationally in cars from 17, and won the Paris 1000km at 21. The combination of family capital, early equipment access, and sibling partnership created an exceptional early advantage stack.
starting_point: Born to a wealthy family in Mexico City; father was a successful railroad broker who encouraged competition and funded the brothers' racing careers.
current_position: Died in 1971 at age 31 in a racing accident at the Norisring, Nuremberg, West Germany; final role: professional racing driver in F1 and sports cars.

trajectory.event: Won Mexican national motorcycle championship on a 125cc Adler.
Made international car racing debut at Nassau driving a Ferrari.
Won the Paris 1000km endurance race with brother Ricardo in a Ferrari 250 GT.
Made Formula One world championship debut at the United States Grand Prix.
Won the South African Grand Prix in a Cooper, his first F1 victory.
Won the 24 Hours of Le Mans in a Ford GT40.
Killed in a racing accident at the Norisring in Nuremberg, West Germany.

name: Jouko Törmänen
milestone_by_age_26: Won the Olympic gold medal in the individual large hill event at the 1980 Lake Placid Winter Olympics at age 25, having previously placed 5th at the 1974 World Championships and won a team silver at the 1978 World Championships.
early_history_summary: Törmänen was born in Rovaniemi, Finland and started ski jumping at age 10 with Ounasvaaran Hiihtoseura. He placed 4th at the 1972 junior European Championships at 18, made his senior international debut at the 1974 World Championships (5th on large hill), competed at the 1976 Winter Olympics, and won a team silver at the 1978 World Championships before his Olympic gold in 1980.
family_context_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. Born in Rovaniemi, Finland.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Finnish ski jumping, Ounasvaaran Hiihtoseura, Rovaniemi, early training
evidence_summary: Törmänen grew up in Rovaniemi, a Finnish ski jumping stronghold, and began jumping at age 10 with the local club Ounasvaaran Hiihtoseura. He was among Finland's top jumpers by 18, benefiting from the Finnish ski jumping pipeline that provided coaching, competition, and facilities. No family background is documented in reviewed sources. His early advantage was primarily institutional and geographic: immersion in the Finnish ski jumping ecosystem from a young age with structured coaching and competition.
starting_point: Born in Rovaniemi, Finland; family background not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Died in 2015 at age 60 in Rovaniemi; final role: chairman of the FIS Ski Jumping Committee.

trajectory.event: Placed 5th on the large hill at the World Championships in Falun, Sweden.
Won a team silver medal at the World Championships.
Won Olympic gold in the individual large hill at the Lake Placid Winter Olympics.

Died on 3 January 2015 in Rovaniemi, Finland.

name: Egil Danielsen
milestone_by_age_26: Won the 1956 Olympic gold medal and set a new world record of 85.71m in the javelin at age 23, having already been Norwegian champion from 1953 to 1957.
early_history_summary: Danielsen was born in Hamar, Norway and was an avid cross-country skier before switching to javelin throwing. He became Norwegian javelin champion starting in 1953 at age 20, finished 10th at the 1954 European Championships, and won the 1956 Olympic gold with a world record throw using a borrowed steel javelin from his Polish friend Janusz Sidło. He won European silver in 1958 at age 25.
family_context_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. Born in Hamar, Norway.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Norwegian athletics, Hamar IL, cross-country skiing background, natural throwing ability
evidence_summary: Danielsen came from Hamar, Norway, and was originally a cross-country skier before switching to javelin. He became Norwegian champion at 20 and won Olympic gold at 23 with a world record throw, aided by a borrowed modern javelin from his friend Janusz Sidło. No family background or financial details are documented. His advantage was modest: the Norwegian athletics system provided a competitive platform, and his natural athletic ability and cross-training from skiing contributed to his throwing power. The Olympic victory itself involved an element of serendipity through Sidło's equipment loan.
starting_point: Born in Hamar, Norway; family background not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Died in 2019 at age 85; worked at the Hamar Fire Brigade after retiring from sports.

trajectory.event: Became Norwegian javelin champion, breaking the 70m barrier.
Won Olympic gold and set a world record of 85.71m at the Melbourne Olympics.
Won European Championships silver medal behind Janusz Sidło.
Competed at the Rome Olympics but did not advance from qualifying; retired from sports.
Died on 29 July 2019 in Hamar, Norway.

name: Galina Chistyakova
milestone_by_age_26: Set the still-standing world record of 7.52m in the long jump on 11 June 1988 at age 25, and won the 1988 Olympic bronze medal in Seoul, having already won the 1985 European Indoor Championships gold at 23.
early_history_summary: Chistyakova was born in Izmail, Ukrainian SSR and took up athletics in 1972 at age 10. She was selected for the Soviet national team in 1979 at age 17, trained at Burevestnik and later CSKA Moscow under coach Vyatscheslav Sokolow. She won the 1985 European Indoor Championships gold at 23, the 1986 European Championships silver, and the 1986 Goodwill Games gold before her world record and Olympic medal in 1988.
family_context_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. Born in Izmail, Ukrainian SSR. Married to retired triple jumper Aleksander Beskrovnyi; later lived in Slovakia.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Soviet national team, CSKA Moscow, Burevestnik, early selection, Sokolow coaching
evidence_summary: Chistyakova was selected for the Soviet national team at 17, benefiting from the elite Soviet sports system that identified and nurtured athletes from a young age. She trained at Burevestnik and CSKA Moscow under coach Vyatscheslav Sokolow, with access to facilities, structured training, and international competition. The Soviet Union was the frontier for women's horizontal jumps in the 1980s. No family background is documented. Her world record of 7.52m, set at 25, has stood for over 35 years, suggesting exceptional physical talent amplified by the Soviet athletic pipeline.
starting_point: Born in Izmail, Ukrainian SSR; family background not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Living in Slovakia with husband, retired from competitive athletics; former world record holder in long jump (7.52m, still standing).

trajectory.event: Selected for the Soviet national athletics team.
Won gold in the long jump at the European Indoor Championships.
Won European Championships silver and Goodwill Games gold in the long jump.
Set the world record of 7.52m in the long jump and won Olympic bronze at the Seoul Olympics.
Won World Indoor Championships gold and set a triple jump world record of 14.52m.
Represented Slovakia at the Atlanta Olympics in long jump and triple jump after gaining Slovak citizenship.

name: Waldemar Legień
milestone_by_age_26: Won the 1988 Olympic gold medal in judo (half-middleweight) at age 25, having previously won the junior European Championships gold in 1981 at 18 and World Championship bronze in 1987 at 24.
early_history_summary: Legień was born in Bytom, Poland and started judo at age 9 in 1973 when his father brought him to GKS Czarni Bytom, coached by Józef Wiśniewski. He won the junior European Championships gold in 1981 at 18, overcame a brief kidney illness, and won World Championship bronze medals in 1987, 1989, and 1991 before his Olympic gold in 1988 at age 25.
family_context_summary: Born in Bytom, Poland; son of Tadeusz and Krystyna. His father brought him to his first judo training at age 9, thinking it was gymnastics rather than a combat sport.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father brought him to judo at age 9 but was not a judo practitioner himself; no family domain expertise in martial arts documented.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Czarni Bytom, Polish judo system, Józef Wiśniewski, early start, national team
evidence_summary: Legień started judo at 9 at GKS Czarni Bytom, a top Polish judo club, under coach Józef Wiśniewski. His father introduced him to the sport but had no domain expertise. The Polish judo system provided a structured pipeline from club to national team, with dedicated coaching from Wiśniewski and junior national team coach Marek Rzepkiewicz. He overcame a kidney illness that tested his determination. By 18 he was a junior European champion, and by 25 an Olympic gold medalist, reflecting 16 years of sustained training in a single discipline.
starting_point: Born in Bytom, Poland; son of Tadeusz and Krystyna; father introduced him to judo at age 9.
current_position: Manager of Racing Club de France in Paris; retired from competitive judo; one of only three judokas to win two Olympic gold medals.

trajectory.event: Won junior European Championships gold in San Marino.

name: Roman Abramovich
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Abramovich was running small-scale trading businesses (plastic toys, dolls, commodities) by his early twenties, but his major wealth came from the Sibneft oil acquisition in 1995 at age 29 and subsequent oligarchic deals.
early_history_summary: Abramovich was born in Saratov, Russian SFSR and orphaned by age 3. He was raised by relatives in Komi, northern Russia, left school at 16, worked as a mechanic, and served in the Red Army. During perestroika in the late 1980s, he started trading plastic toys and consumer goods, set up a doll-making company with his first wife in 1988, and founded multiple small trading companies in the early 1990s. His breakthrough came through partnership with Boris Berezovsky and the 1995 Sibneft acquisition.
family_context_summary: Orphaned by age 3; mother Irina was a music teacher who died when Roman was 1, father Aaron was killed in a construction crane accident when Roman was 3. Raised by uncle and grandparents in Komi, northern Russia, in modest conditions.
parent_family_domain_summary: No parental domain expertise transferred; parents died when Abramovich was very young. Mother was a music teacher, father worked in an economic council.
evidence_summary: Abramovich was orphaned by age 3 and raised in modest conditions by relatives in northern Russia. By his early twenties he was trading small goods during perestroika, but these were small-scale enterprises. His major wealth and influence came after age 26 through the Sibneft acquisition in 1995 and partnership with Boris Berezovsky. name: Kitarō
milestone_by_age_26: Released his first solo album Astral Voyage (Tenku) in 1978 at age 25, which quickly gained a cult following, after previously performing and recording with the Far East Family Band whose albums were produced by Klaus Schulze.
early_history_summary: Kitarō was born Masanori Takahashi in Toyohashi, Aichi, Japan to a family of Shinto-Buddhist farmers. He played electric guitar in a high school R&B band, then moved to Tokyo where he joined the Far East Family Band in the early 1970s. During a 1972 trip to Europe with the band, he met German synthesist Klaus Schulze, who produced two of the band's albums. Kitarō built his first synthesizer and began his solo career in 1978 with Astral Voyage.
family_context_summary: Born to a family of Shinto-Buddhist farmers in Toyohashi, Japan. Parents initially opposed his musical career and arranged a job at a local company, which he silently refused to attend.
parent_family_domain_summary: No parental domain expertise in music; family were farmers. Parents opposed his musical ambitions.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Klaus Schulze, Far East Family Band, self-taught synthesizer, defied parents
evidence_summary: Kitarō came from a farming family with no musical background; his parents actively opposed his career choice. His key early advantage was meeting Klaus Schulze in 1972, who became a mentor and producer for the Far East Family Band. Kitarō was largely self-taught, building his own synthesizer after discovering Schulze's work. The Far East Family Band provided a collaborative peer environment. His defiance of family expectations and self-directed learning in synthesizer music created a distinctive path, but his early advantage stack was modest compared to institutionally trained musicians.
starting_point: Born to a family of Shinto-Buddhist farmers in Toyohashi, Japan; parents opposed his musical career.
current_position: Active musician and composer; Grammy-winning new age artist with 16 Grammy nominations and a Golden Globe; based in Japan.

trajectory.event: Met German synthesist Klaus Schulze during a Far East Family Band tour of Europe, inspiring his synthesizer work.
Released first solo album Astral Voyage (Tenku), which gained a cult following.

Won the Grammy Award for Best New Age Album for Thinking of You.
